Project in Zambia shows how teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects

W omen making their way in patriarchal societies down the ages have always had to wield their meagre economic power deftly. New evidence from a fascinating research project in Zambia suggests that’s a skill that can be learned.

A team of female US academics have been gathering data for more than a decade, which shows that teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects.

Groups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks – delivered by local young women who had completed their schooling and had been closely involved in developing the curriculum.

Follow-up analysis suggests the girls who took these lessons are continuing to reap economic benefits, more than a decade later.

Measured against a control group, who were given “empowerment” classes by the same coaches, but without the negotiation work, the young women tended to stay in school longer; were more likely to graduate from college; and less likely to marry a much older man.

Prof Corinne Low, whose day job is teaching economics at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, has been involved in the project from its inception. She says back then that the Zambian government was interested in understanding what was preventing girls from attending secondary school.

Low and her colleagues carried out focus groups, suspecting they might hear that girls found school boring. Instead, participants told them they were keen to attend, but unable to convince their parents or other relatives to pay the fees.

“There was misunderstanding in the relationships that they had – it would be, ‘I know that my son is going to help support me,’ or, ‘my son is going to look out for the family, but my daughter, she’s going to get into trouble with boys.’”

That convinced Low and colleague Nava Ashraf that the girls could benefit from similar negotiating skills to those taught, in a very different context, to sharp-elbowed MBA students in the US.

The most important insight in the six two-hour classes, she says, is that instead of seeing the person you’re negotiating with as an enemy, a more successful approach is to understand their perspective, and tackle problems together.

“We really emphasised this sort of understanding somebody else’s interests; understanding somebody else’s problems,” she says.

It’s an idea that would be familiar to former trade union negotiators Louise Haigh and Angela Rayner, now two of the most powerful women in the UK government.

“You can’t just go in and tell these girls: ‘You have to stay in school.’ You need to give them tools that are actually going to change the outcomes here,” Low says.

Perhaps counterintuitively, given the ultimate aim is female empowerment, the content of the curriculum also leant heavily on the need for respecting the reality of existing hierarchies – for now at least.

“In Zambia, there was a lot of generational hierarchy and it was really important to show respect for parents. We talked to the girls and said: ‘If you’re going to approach your parents to ask them for something, what are some of the ways you show respect?’ And they said: ‘Oh well, I might kneel down, and I might address them formally, and I might wear a traditional wrapper – a chitenge.’”

after newsletter promotion

“The irony is, right – what kind of empowerment programme is teaching girls to kneel down?” she laughs. But she adds: “The reality is that these girls do not have the power in their household and we can’t pretend that they do.”

Subsequent surveys showed the girls’ parents felt their relationships had improved. “The parents recorded that the girls were more respectful, were more likely to do chores around the household, that they were more understanding,” Low recalls.

She and her colleagues are now working towards a 15-year follow-up with that original cohort, now women in their 20s; but their approach has since been incorporated into the Zambian curriculum, and replicated in several other countries.

Most recently – and strikingly – the NGO Free to Run has been using an adapted version of the material in online classes that have recently reached about 1,200 girls in Afghanistan, whose lives and opportunities have been brutally curtailed by the Taliban.

While almost all prospect of economic advancement for them is blocked, Sana Mahmud, the charity’s global programmes manager, says the curriculum is helping young women to manage their mental health, and to achieve small freedoms in the grim context of the regime.

“It’s a very useful skill inside the household to negotiate with parents, even if it’s small things like permission to visit a friend,” she says.

And she adds: “Sometimes the young women would leave their homes to go out in the market or do errands, and some of them have even been stopped by members of the Taliban to ask: ‘Why are you here? What are you doing?’ and we realised that the skill of negotiation is probably the best for them to safely talk about what they’re doing, why they’re there.” The course is taught by four Afghan women, and feedback from participants has been “amazing”, Mahmud says.

Of course, the wider economic and political system matters far more than each woman’s success in navigating her way through it, and the situation in Afghanistan is bleak. We should all be working towards a world in which the patriarchy is – as the placards and pin badges have it – smashed.

But giving more girls skills that might help them further their own interests in the world as it is today seems a wise investment in that future.

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed nearly 600 people, left another 1,900 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.

“The trauma of this event is enormous,” David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal , said on Friday.

“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need. The death toll is very high and unfortunately likely to continue to rise.”

The deadly floods occurred on Wednesday morning after an enormous section ⁠of a glacier in the Himalayas broke loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive surge of water, mud, rock and ice that thundered down rivers and valleys. The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed power stations, roads and bridges.

Nepal’s steep slopes and the lush valleys below are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events, such as intense monsoons, and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.

“The damage is just incredible,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN resident coordinator for Nepal, said on Friday, adding that more than 40 bridges had been destroyed or badly damaged and “over 40km of road completely destroyed”.

By Friday afternoon, the death toll stood at 584 people: 579 in Nepal and five across the border in Tibet, China. Authorities in Nepal said 1,942 people were still missing , including hundreds of foreign nationals who were in the area to work, trek with guides or make a pilgrimage.

Rescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Indian border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

Rescuers were forced to suspend operations on Friday morning after a dam of debris overflowed on Friday, increasing the risk of further flooding. Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses.

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the border overflowed.

Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.

Nearby, people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

Most areas battered by the flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, from where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned in a matter of minutes.

The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.

Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search and rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of bridges and roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search and rescue teams to assist in the operation.

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with Tibet.

“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.

But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only five deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

However, Kevin Warsh didn’t say if interest rates would change in coming months, as inflation remains stubborn

The US Federal Reserve is not done fighting high inflation, its chair, Kevin Warsh, said in his first major speech in the role on Friday, emphasizing that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”.

Warsh did not indicate where the Fed will take interest rates in the coming months, despite US inflation remaining stubbornly above the central bank’s 2% target amid the war in Iran. But his speech was taken by markets as a signal that rates may rise in the coming months, a move that may put him at odds with Donald Trump , who has aggressively called for rates to be cut.

The Fed chair painted a rosy view of the economy that contrasts with recent data. He said the economy “appears to have strengthened” given how it has held up to shocks.

“On that score, both Main Street and Wall Street have been resilient,” Warsh said at the Fed’s annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday.

The Jackson Hole symposium has typically served as a platform for Fed chairs to offer clarity on the central bank’s general direction. For example, former Fed chair Jerome Powell foreshadowed rate cuts at his keynote address last year.

But Warsh on Friday insisted the days of such “forward guidance” were over, saying that the practice was adopted by the Fed during the 2008 financial crisis. “As with other legacies of crises past, I believe that the practice has overstayed its welcome,” he said.

Markets are still expected to carefully gauge Warsh’s speech for signs of the Fed’s next move. At the central bank’s last board meeting in July, three out of 12 voting members wanted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point – the first time in a decade so many board members shared dissent over a policy position. But a majority of the members voted to hold rates, which currently sit at a range of 3.5% to 3.75%, steady.

Since he was appointed in May, Warsh has had to strike a delicate balance between managing an economy that has been shaken by higher oil prices brought on by the war in Iran without provoking the ire of the White House. Trump has continued to insist the Fed should lower interest rates, despite economists who warn that that would further exacerbate inflation. After hitting a three-year high of 4.2% in May, US inflation cooled to 3.4% in July – still 1% higher than figures seen last year.

Warsh said progress on inflation over the past several years has been “modest”, and though price readings from over the summer came in better than expected, they did not indicate that “underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.

after newsletter promotion

The US bond market has been particularly sensitive to higher inflation, with the yield on 10-year notes hitting its highest level since 2007 in recent weeks. Yields briefly went down after the US treasury announced a big debt buy-back scheme , though the relief proved to be temporary. Rising rates in the US have driven yields higher abroad – bond rates in the UK, Germany, France and Japan have all hit their highest levels in decades. Meanwhile, the US gross national debt topped $40tn for the first time in history last week.

In reaction to Warsh’s opening remarks, the two-year and 10-year US treasury yields increased slightly, while the 30-year treasury remained largely the same. The S&P 500 remained leveled while the Dow Jones ticked down slightly.

Families are rushing to Nepal to search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing, as fears mount over the risk of a second wave of flooding in the region.

The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday , thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 538 people, while more than 1,500 remain missing.

Among them are hundreds of foreign tourists who were visiting the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims for its natural beauty and religious significance.

Relatives of missing Britons have shared their devastation as they desperately try to reach their loved ones who were last seen in the Rasuwa district, where power and communication lines are down. Many are scrambling to book flights to Kathmandu, the Nepalese capital. On Friday, authorities in Nepal and China issued warnings about the risk of a second wave of flooding. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake had formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border, posing a risk of “sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake that had formed after debris blocked a river at the site was also rising and ‌at risk of bursting.

Rescuers were forced to suspend their search for survivors, while residents who had returned to Rasuwa were told to evacuate their homes. Many were seen fleeing up the hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river.

In a video on YouTube, Jaggi Vasudev, known as Sadhguru, a spiritual leader who founded the nonprofit Isha Foundation, told followers at the foundation’s camp at Saga in Tibet , China, that 80 members of an Isha group returning from Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists, were missing, including nine British people.

Among them was Neetu Goyal Tiwari, 51. Her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC that completing the pilgrimage was “her dream”. Neetu’s nephew, Anmol Goyal, said she had been travelling with a friend, and that her last known location was at the immigration centre on the Tibet-Nepal border. He said she had been added to the Nepalese government’s official list of missing persons.

The family have been desperately phoning contacts in Nepal in an attempt to find her, though they increasingly believe her to still be in China. As many of them are based in India, it is difficult for them to obtain visas to search for her. Goyal said her husband and daughter remained in the UK for now.

“We’re not sure what the next second holds and what we should do from our end, because we’re trying to reach everyone we can,” he said. “She was a very fun-loving woman [and] really had a great heart. I really hope she comes back soon.”

The Telegraph reported that an NHS psychiatrist, Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims on Isha Foundation’s journey to Mount Kailash. The group’s last-known location was an immigration centre in Timure, in the mudslide’s direct path. His wife, Manjula Atmakur, who arrived in Kathmandu to search for him on Friday, told the newspaper she was disappointed by the British government’s response to the disaster.

Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, 53, from Slough, was among 27 travellers in its group who were unaccounted for.

Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he was booking the next flight to Kathmandu after the Home Office had failed to confirm whether Leena was on its missing persons list. “Even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there,” he said. “She must be in trauma.” Also missing are an A-level student from Surrey, Spandan Sahu, 18, and his father, Santosh Sahu, 46, the chief executive of the UK pharmaceutical technology company Charac; Spandan’s mother, Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44; and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.

Mahadev Semwal, a friend of Sahu’s for about 15 years, said: “I had WhatsApp communication with him on Monday: they were going to Nepal then Manasarovar in Tibet.

“When I heard on Wednesday about the flooding, I lost contact with him – when I am trying to message him it is getting delivered but not read.

“Our heart says they are safe somewhere. It’s possible because the communication is jammed.

“But when you see the videos, it is unbelievable. It feels so bad.”

Also confirmed missing was Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse from Dartford, Kent, who left for Nepal last Saturday on a religious journey. Deepesh Patel told the Press Association that his parents, Bipin Patel, 66, and Mala Patel, 60, from Coventry, were missing after flying to Nepal on 22 August for a pilgrimage. His brother Anant Patel told Sky News he was “shocked” at the lack of information on their whereabouts.

Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he had not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy. Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit.

“We’re not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week,” Kolagatla added.

Tatjana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, told the BBC she had not been able to contact her sister, Julija Jakovicka, who was attending a yoga and meditation retreat near the Nepal-Tibet border when flash flooding hit.

Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he had not heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, or sister-in-law, Ankita Chandra, 35, who had gone on a pilgrimage.

Ranjan added: “We don’t know if they crossed the border … We don’t have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated.”

The tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said it had been unable to make contact with a party of 12 Britons aged 13 to 65 who had booked a tour to Mount Kailash in Tibet, and were in the vicinity when the flash floods hit.

Sunil Amin, from Croydon in south London, shared with the Daily Mail the “horrible, horrible feeling” of repeatedly trying to phone his wife, Hema Amin, 63, who was on a pilgrimage with Alpine Eco Trek from Nepal to Tibet with her sister. “I’m devastated,” he said.

The Trekkers’ Society, which organises tours across Nepal, Tibet and Bhutan, said nine UK nationals on a pilgrimage had gone missing. The organisation confirmed that four men and boys aged between 14 and 50 and five women aged 40 to 53 were unaccounted for.

Himalayan Glacier US said it had lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff, including two Britons, who were also on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, regarded as the spiritual home of the Hindu god Shiva.

The tour operator Kailash Journeys confirmed it had not been able to account for seven UK nationals – five women and two men aged between 18 and 55 – who were travelling with it. Leaf Holidays, which runs Himalayan treks and expeditions from Kathmandu, wrote in a Facebook post that its group of 55 travellers remained missing, including four British citizens, Tara and Babar Gurung and Thaneswar and Tejkumari Gurung, who have not been heard from since Tuesday.

Twelve of the missing British citizens were on a tour to Mount Kailash led by Nabhi Nandan Das, a 64-year-old Hindu priest who works at the Sanatan Mandir and community centre in Surrey, the Telegraph reported. He is understood to have been leading 11 Britons on a tour that was due to visit Kailash and Lake Mansarovar, two Hindu holy sites in Tibet.

Pramod Poudel, who runs a Nepalese street food company in Sussex, told the Daily Mail his wife, Sumitra, mother, Tulisa, brother Pradip and uncle Madav were all missing. His father, Purusottam, has been found alive.

The Non-Resident Nepali Association in the UK launched an emergency fundraising appeal on Thursday and more than £12,000 has been raised.

Rajendra Pudasaini, a nurse in Essex who is president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association UK, said Nepal was witnessing an “irreplaceable loss” and Nepal was “paying the price for global warming”.

Pudasaini told BBC Radio 4 Today’s programme that many of his family members were missing. “My godson, we found the body yesterday morning, you know, he (was) just buried under the mud at his house, and yes, lots of other dead bodies being found.”

He added: “It’s a very difficult situation to describe, actually.”

stories.body:
Scale of devastation emerges in Nepal as reporters reach disaster area, but Chinese state media focus more on rescue efforts

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

In the days since an enormous glacier in the Himalayas snapped away from a mountaintop and cascaded into the valley below, the true scale of the devastation caused by the flash floods in Nepal and Tibet is still unfolding.

But the picture is emerging far more quickly in Nepal than in China, where strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.

The floods devastated villages along the Himalayan border region that straddles Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. On Friday, the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, while in China it was just five, despite the fact that the villages around the Gyirong border crossing are home to several thousand people.

In Nepal, journalists rushed to get as close to the disaster zone as possible to interview survivors and rescue workers. Villagers provided minute-by-minute accounts of what happened when the floods, the exact cause of which is still being studied by scientists, tore through their homes.

In China, state media carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.

Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country. Sporadic protests, including self-immolations, by Tibetans calling for more autonomy and religious freedom have been cracked down on by the authorities. International journalists cannot visit Tibet apart from on tightly choreographed government tours. Many Tibetans are not allowed passports and have very limited contact with the outside world. Tibetans can be punished for speaking to journalists. Human rights groups have for years criticised Beijing’s policies on Tibetan language and culture, which activists say are under attack.

That makes independent assessments of how the flash floods have affected the Tibetan side of the border difficult.

“Everything about Tibet is seen through the national security prism. And therefore nobody is going to say anything or report anything that has not been cleared from the very top,” said Steve Tsang, the director of the China Institute at Soas University of London.

For anyone on the ground, “you can’t report a higher figure of deaths, even if you have seen more bodies yourself, until the official statement says that the figure has gone up”.

China’s tight controls on information are limiting international coverage of its relief efforts. That may mean China is missing an opportunity to tell its own good news story.

Chinese emergency services, including the People’s Liberation Army, are vastly better resourced than their Nepalese counterparts. Navigating the difficult, mountainous terrain where conditions are still unsafe requires specialised expertise. China has dispatched hundreds of emergency service personnel but there is scant detail on what they are doing. “The Chinese have missed a trick,” Tsang said. But “they don’t have that confidence. Their instinct is control.”

Still, China has been keen to stress that the disaster is a national priority. China’s leader, Xi Jinping, chaired a meeting on Friday to direct rescue work, according to state media. Xi called on the authorities to “make every effort to search for missing people from China and abroad”. He also dispatched his number two, premier Li Qiang, to visit the affected area. According to the state-run Xinhua news agency, Li “emphasised that General Secretary Xi Jinping is deeply concerned about the people in the disaster-stricken areas”.

stories.body:
Hundreds of foreigners were in area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages when disaster struck

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.

Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.

Here is how different countries have been affected.

Nepal

Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.

China

State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.

India

India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.

US

The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.

Malaysia

Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.

Ukraine

Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.

Australia

The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.

Britain

Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.

Canada

The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada .

South Korea

South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.

Singapore

Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.

Germany

The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.

Russia

The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.

South Africa

The NTB said six South Africans were missing.

Latvia

The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.

Japan

Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.

New Zealand

Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.

France

The NTB said four French citizens were missing.

Belgium

The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.

Spain

The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.

Others

The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

stories.body:
Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races

Every day $1bn worth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry.

News this week of Donald Trump’s escalating trade spat with Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”.

“We don’t need Canada , they need us,” Trump declared.

But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped.

Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program.

By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices.

Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump.

“I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said.

Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as they pay on average over $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada.

The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group.

“Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added.

This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation.

The tariffs and the unpopular Iran war’s contribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery.

“El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.”

In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis.

“Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.”

El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation.

“If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those.

“Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added.

Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Anderson estimated tariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025.

The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster.

“This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said.

The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade.

But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster.

The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state.

“Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added.

Indeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”.

The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.”

The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef.

“What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.”

Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.

However, the typically pro-Trump Detroit chamber of commerce did not mince words.

“Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most.

“Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.”

Roadmap for increasing department’s share of GDP will be deferred until next year’s review

The chancellor will delay setting out when the UK will meet the target of allocating 3% of GDP on defence until next year’s spending review, the Treasury has confirmed.

John Healey resigned as defence secretary in June under Keir Starmer’s leadership, accusing the prime minister of being “unable” and the Treasury “unwilling” to “commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country”.

However, since succeeding Rachel Reeves following Andy Burnham’s arrival at No 10, Healey has declined to set a date for meeting the 3% target, which he had previously insisted should be hit by 2030.

Treasury sources confirmed that instead, the focus in Healey’s first budget on 28 October, would be fully funding the defence investment plan.

The three-year DIP was one of Starmer’s final announcements – but about £1.2bn a year was left unaccounted for, with Healey’s predecessor Reeves suggesting the money would have to be found through cuts in other Whitehall departments.

The Treasury confirmed on Friday that there would be no further detail about the timeline in the budget. A spending review is expected to be held next year but no date has yet been set.

A government spokesperson said: “The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe. The prime minister and chancellor are committed to fully funding the defence investment plan. At the spending review we will set out a pathway to meet our Nato commitment of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and will set a target date to hit 3% on that path.”

Defence spending is on track to reach 2.7% of GDP by 2030, funded partly by Starmer’s decision to cut the UK’s aid spending.

Healey had previously said that this figure should rise to 3% urgently, given the growing global conflicts and security risks. He wrote in his resignation letter to Starmer in June : “As we have regularly discussed, I am certain that a headmark date for 3% of GDP on defence in 2030 is what Britain must set.” So far, the prime minister, Burnham, has refused to commit to the 3% target.

In an interview with Sky News on Friday, Healey said fiscal discipline was the “first priority” for any chancellor.

Healey and his colleagues will discuss the prospects for global growth, against the backdrop of continued high energy prices, volatile government bond markets and the US-Canada trade war.

Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?

The international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet on Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting.

The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 469 people and left more than 1,300 missing.

Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

Nepali army helicopter rescue teams were working on Friday to rescue about 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by the devastating flood.

“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said Nepal army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”

The prime minister’s office said the army was working in tough conditions and had already rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel amid the risky conditions.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the border with India. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

Videos from Wednesday showed a massive wall of water crashing down on the border as people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape.

Trucks were overturned and houses, roads ⁠and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.

Tom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water.

Nepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst.

Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home.

“A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.”

Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.”

Kamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.”

Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.”

People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.

Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.

The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”

More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.

Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.

Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.

Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, causing the flood of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.

Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover.

“Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.”

Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said.

Scant information emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution.

Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups and experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.”

She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”.

stories.title: Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying unlike Starmer
stories.summary: Burnham has called for all views to be respected as MPs vote in two weeks on legalising assisted dying in England and Wales.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham has reminded MPs that all views must be respected

Published 28 August 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has revealed he will not vote on the assisted dying bill for England and Wales unlike his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

MPs are likely to get the chance to debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill in two weeks' time.

The bill is identical to the one put to Parliament last year, where it passed in the House of Commons but stalled in the Lords after an unprecedented number of amendments meant it ran out of time .

Burnham said he has his "own personal views on the issue" but it was "a matter for Parliament to decide". Starmer voted in favour of the previous bill when he was PM but did not campaign in favour of it, remaining officially neutral.

Writing to Labour MPs on Friday, Burnham said: "My role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of Parliament in this area – whether that is to change the law or not.

"I also do not want to unduly influence the debate as prime minister and for every colleague to know it is a genuinely free vote.

"For these reasons, I have taken the decision that it is most appropriate for me not to vote at Second Reading."

He added that "there is no single right position" and it was an "incredibly important and personal debate".

"It is vital that those different views are treated with dignity and respect," he wrote.

While his abstension is a departure from Starmer's support , Burnham stressed that the government as an entity would officially remain neutral on the bill.

When he was Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham indicated he was in favour of assisted dying in principle.

But in June he suggested it would be challenging to implement before social and palliative care were improved.

The assisted dying law would allow adults over the age of 18 who are expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Ministers told to avoid comment

Burnham has also told ministers they can vote as they wish but, in a separate letter on Friday, he told them they "should avoid being part of the public debate and should not express views about the implications of the bill for their department's responsibilities".

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper previously voted in favour of assisted dying, but her predecessor Wes Streeting had openly voiced concerns about the implications for the NHS.

Supporters of the assisted dying bill - brought by Labour MP Lauren Edwards - are hoping it will pass the Commons unamended.

This is because an amended bill in the Commons would remove powers under the Parliament Acts to override the Lords and make it law if they refuse to back it.

MPs in favour of the bill hope Lords would vote in favour, if presented the choice of some sceptical amendments versus an entirely unamended bill becoming law.

It comes after the Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments, mainly from opponents, during the previous bill earlier this year.

That prompted assisted dying campaigner Dame Esther Rantzen, who has terminal cancer, to accuse opponents of trying to sabotage rather than scrutinise it.

Opponents of assisted dying have vowed to continue scrutinising the bill.

A separate bill that would have legalised assisted dying in Scotland was rejected by the Scottish Parliament in March 2026 .

stories.title: Trump blacklisting of "woke" Anthropic deemed illegal by federal judge
stories.summary: Anthropic refused to support lethal autonomous warfare and mass surveillance.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Anthropic refused to support lethal autonomous warfare and mass surveillance.

The Trump administration’s blacklisting of Anthropic was illegal, a federal judge ruled in an order vacating government directives against the use of the firm’s AI technology.

The government illegally retaliated against Anthropic by designating it a supply-chain risk to national security, said yesterday’s ruling by Judge Rita Lin in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The maker of Claude AI technology was barred by the US after it refused to drop restrictions on the use of its products for lethal autonomous warfare and mass surveillance of Americans, the ruling said.

“The undisputed record shows that the challenged actions constituted unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment,” Lin wrote in an order that granted key portions of Anthropic’s motion for summary judgment.

As Lin noted, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “ordered all federal agencies to permanently stop using Anthropic’s products, and banned all defense contractors from doing any business with Anthropic, even if unrelated to the military.” Lin vacated those government actions and ordered the Trump administration to rescind the directives that she deemed illegal.

National security is not blank check to retaliate

“Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice, the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless,” Lin wrote, referring to the Trump administration’s preferred name for the Department of Defense. “The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” she added.

The Trump administration provided only a “slim” justification to the court, Lin wrote, stating that the federal defendants “have now backed away from the thrust of their risk assessment, which relied on Anthropic having backdoor access to its technology once deployed in a national security system. It is now clear that Anthropic undisputedly lacks any such access and that, as Defendants concede, Anthropic’s technology is itself no riskier to the national security than any other ‘black box’ artificial intelligence model.”

Anthropic sued the Trump administration in March, saying the government blacklisted it in retaliation after Anthropic refused to let its Claude AI models be used for autonomous warfare and mass surveillance of Americans. Anthropic said the First Amendment gives it “the right to express its views—both publicly and to the government—about the limitations of its own AI services and important issues of AI safety,” and that the government process for designating it a supply-chain risk did not comply with procedures mandated by Congress.

The White House responded to Anthropic’s lawsuit by saying that “President Trump will never allow a radical left, woke company to jeopardize our national security by dictating how the greatest and most powerful military in the world operates.”

Two courts probe blacklist

The Trump administration won an early ruling from Trump-appointed judges in the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which denied Anthropic’s emergency motion for a stay. But the DC Circuit appeals court went on to hold oral arguments and is still reviewing the case while the sides continue to submit briefs.

Anthropic had meanwhile also sued in the Northern District of California and won multiple rulings from Lin, a Biden appointee. Lin issued a preliminary injunction on March 26, prohibiting the government from implementing the Trump and Hegseth orders.

The preliminary-injunction ruling said that nothing in the relevant US law “supports the Orwellian notion that an American company may be branded a potential adversary and saboteur of the US for expressing disagreement with the government.” The March injunction did not require the Trump administration to use Anthropic products as long as its “actions are consistent with applicable regulations, statutes, and constitutional provisions.”

Lin yesterday ruled that the Trump administration actions were arbitrary and capricious, violating Administrative Procedure Act requirements that govern how federal agencies may impose regulations. She found that Anthropic does not meet the legal definition of a supply-chain risk, which is limited to “the risk that an adversary may sabotage, maliciously introduce unwanted function, or otherwise subvert… a covered system.”

“The plain text of the statute is directed at covert acts or hacks, not overt, public positions regarding contract terms,” Lin wrote.

Tech industry welcomes ruling

The Trump administration could appeal the ruling and is continuing to make its case in the DC Circuit Court of Appeals. We contacted the White House and will update this article if it provides a comment.

The Computer & Communications Industry Association, a lobby group for tech firms, said it is “encouraged by this outcome, as this case matters to anyone doing business with the US government. By bypassing standard procurement to target Anthropic in this fashion, the Pentagon’s action deeply concerned any company that has contracts with the government.”

Government use of Anthropic hasn’t completely stopped. “Despite the ban, government agencies continued using Anthropic’s tools as the White House and the company ‌gradually mended ties ahead of Anthropic’s planned IPO,” Reuters wrote .

Anthropic said in a statement provided to Ars that “we welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful. We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology.”

stories.title: FM calls for referendum powers as draft independence bill published
stories.summary: The draft bill would be introduced into Parliament if the Scottish government secured the necessary powers from the UK government.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Scotland voted no in the 2014 independence referendum

Published 28 August 2026

The Scottish government has published its draft independence referendum bill, setting out the details of the proposed question and who would be allowed to vote.

The short document has been released ahead of the first minister setting out his legislative plans for the year on Tuesday.

John Swinney called on the UK government to "respect the voice of the Scottish people and parliament and transfer the necessary powers" in order to hold the vote.

Since 2014 successive UK governments have opposed any further referendums and Downing Street recently said a fresh poll was "off limits" .

A UK government spokesperson said: "The prime minister made clear to the first minister in their first meeting that another referendum on independence was off the table. It would take our focus away from growing the economy and helping families with the cost of living.

"We will continue working with the Scottish government and other partners to build a fairer country for everyone."

Burnham tells Swinney independence is 'off limits' at Commonwealth Games meeting Published 23 July

Scotland previously voted against becoming an independent country by 55% to 45%.

In 2022 the UK Supreme Court ruled that any further vote would require the agreement of the UK government.

The proposed ballot paper for a second referendum would ask: "Should Scotland be an independent country?" and voters would mark an "X" against options Yes or No.

The draft bill would be introduced into parliament if the Scottish government secured approval from the UK government.

The document would include a date for the referendum once it was put before Holyrood.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham met First Minister John Swinney ahead of the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony in Glasgow last month

The SNP had promised to publish the draft legislation in their first 100 days in government after the Scottish election in May.

Swinney said: "The world has changed fundamentally since 2014. So has the UK, and so has Scotland.

"Scotland is ready. The Scottish people are ready. It is time the UK government delivered."

The first minister said he would have "more to say about Scotland's constitutional future in the coming weeks".

He added: "Fundamentally, nobody will take better decisions about Scotland's future than the people who live here.

"That future belongs to the people of Scotland - and no-one else."

In line with current legislation, registered voters over the age of 16, as well as qualifying foreign nationals, would be able to vote in a second referendum.

Campaigners gathered in Edinburgh ahead of the 2014 independence referendum

Earlier this year, Prof Sir John Curtice of Strathclyde University said Scotland remained "more or less divided down the middle on the subject".

He added: "Sometimes yes is a little ahead of no, sometimes it's the other way around. Yes is typically stronger than it was in the actual referendum."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Swinney ahead of the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony in Glasgow last month.

Afterwards a Downing Street statement said: "The prime minister stated up front that another referendum on independence was off limits because it would take our focus away from growing the economy and helping families with the cost of living."

Scottish Labour acting leader Jackie Baillie said: "The people of Scotland deserve far better than this failing SNP government that is more interested in empty gestures and grandstanding than it is in improving the lives of people across the country."

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay called on Swinney to "abandon this tedious obsession and get on with the day job."

stories.title: Ex-council chief investigated in DUP mayor clothing probe
stories.summary: Anne Donaghy is one of three people referred to prosecutors for consideration over alleged misconduct in public office.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Anne Donaghy pictured outside court earlier this week

Published 28 August 2026

An ex-council chief executive is a subject in a police investigation into a former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) mayor's clothing expenses.

Anne Donaghy is one of three people referred to prosecutors for consideration over alleged misconduct in public office at Mid and East Antrim Borough Council.

It is the latest case surrounding its handling of Freedom of Information (FoI) legislation after Donaghy was convicted on Wednesday of two charges over the deletion of an email to former DUP leader Arlene Foster.

Donaghy's solicitor told BBC News NI the allegations would be "met with the same robustness as this week's proceedings which are now under appeal".

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed a file has been submitted to the Public Prosecution Service (PPS) for consideration.

Police said the investigation was in respect of two women aged 56 and 42, and a 57-year-old man.

None of the three are the former DUP mayor whose expenses were examined.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that "as far as I'm aware there are no issues that pertain to my colleagues or my party".

"These are issues for Ms Donaghy to deal with," he told the BBC Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme .

Expenses cheque

The case centres on questions over clothing expenses claimed by Audrey Wales, 80, who was mayor between 2016 and 2017.

The Ballymena councillor spent more than £2,300, but the council did not disclose the full cost when asked for details in an FoI request.

Instead its response in 2019 said Wales had spent just £190.

The entire bill was only revealed in a second FoI in 2022.

In a statement in 2022, Wales said she had sent a cheque in 2019 reimbursing the council for most of the spending to stop "electorally motivated questions".

The cheque was received by Donaghy, but was never cashed.

Wales, who sent a second cheque in 2021 upon learning the first had not been processed, said that "at all times" she acted in line with "guidance from council officials".

The council in 2022 commissioned a Belfast-based firm to conduct an investigation.

It found the council's FoI response involved "a deliberate manipulation", according to a copy leaked to the Belfast Telegraph. , external

Donaghy has previously denied being involved in discussions about the FOI and said an email she sent referring to the cheque showed that she intended to cash it.

When asked at the time whether it was examining the case, the PSNI said detectives were continuing to "investigate suspected offences of misconduct in public office and under the Freedom of Information Act 2000".

In an update, a PSNI spokesperson told BBC News NI: "A file was submitted to the PPS in January 2025 concerning this investigation in respect of two females aged 56 and 42, and a 57-year-old man."

It is understood the investigation file relates to alleged offences including misconduct in a public office.

The PPS does not comment on any evidence in a file while it remains under consideration.

The case emerges after Donaghy was on Wednesday convicted of two charges connected to deleting or attempting to delete an email to prevent disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act.

The 56-year-old, of Clonmore Road, Dungannon, was fined £1,500. She was cleared of a third charge of trying to have an email deleted.

'Vehemently contest'

On Wednesday Donaghy's solicitor said she "maintains her innocence" and would "vehemently contest" the findings.

In a further statement on the clothing expenses case, her solicitor said: "These are allegations of some considerable vintage stretching back a number of years.

"If they ever materialise into anything then they will be met with the same robustness as this week's proceedings which are now under appeal."

Mid and East Antrim Borough Council has said it will "carefully consider the outcome and any implications arising" from this week's trial.

It added the council is "committed to the highest standards of governance, transparency and information management".

The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) has urged public bodies to ensure they have proper arrangements to "protect" official records.

In a statement an ICO spokesperson said: "Public authorities must have robust records management practices in place and take appropriate steps to preserve information that is subject to a request under Freedom of Information legislation."

stories.title: Here's what we know about the "space academy" Trump just announced
stories.summary: "It's called the US Space Academy. That's a big deal."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“It’s called the US Space Academy. That’s a big deal.”

During a visit to Johnson Space Center, President Trump on Friday signed an executive order to establish a new commission with the purpose of creating the first national space academy.

“It’s clear that we will need to educate and train an entire generation of skilled service members, engineers, and civil operators, and everything else to do what we have to do,” Trump said. “I will sign an executive order to begin the process of creating a new national academy. It’s called the US Space Academy. That’s a big deal.”

The proposed United States Space Academy would fall under the jurisdiction of NASA, and according to US space officials, is not intended be a traditional service academy in the sense that it educates and trains officers for the armed services, such as the Air Force Academy.

Trump signed the executive order as part of a ceremony in Houston during which he awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the four astronauts who flew on Artemis II earlier this year.

Seeking to modernize NASA

This initiative is being spearheaded by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who included the development of an “academy” to seed the future NASA workforce as part of his Project Athena plan to revamp US civil space efforts.

The goal is to create a top-tier educational institution with free tuition and, in return, graduating students to fulfill a service commitment of several years. Graduates will have the choice of going into the US Space Force, but the majority of slots will be allocated to NASA and civilian positions, according to people familiar with the project.

Isaacman has been seeking to modernize NASA and help the space agency find its way at a time when the US commercial space industry is taking an increased role in the types of activities—launch, crewed spaceflight, space stations, lunar activities—that were once the sole province of the space agency. Isaacman has sought to increasingly lean on the commercial industry where it is excelling and focus NASA resources on cutting-edge initiatives, like developing a base on the surface of the Moon.

The academy idea remains in its formative stages but is likely to include curricula that cover human and non-human spaceflight operations, ground control operations, space vehicle design, orbital debris mitigation, and related disciplines. The goal is to create a new generation of technical leaders who can support ongoing exploration efforts, both in commercial spaceflight and in ensuring that the US government maintains a global lead in doing hard things in space.

This would be an entirely new academy, perhaps similar in design to the US Merchant Marine Academy, which is based in Kings Point, New York. Students would apply after high school for admission and be taught by leaders in both the civil and commercial spaces. Students would earn a four-year degree. No location has been chosen for the academy, but it may be near existing NASA facilities or workforce expertise. “I’m going to be choosing a location very shortly,” Trump said Friday.

Blurring lines between military and civil space?

A former deputy administrator of NASA, Lori Garver, said the idea of creating a space academy could be helpful for the US space program and its future workforce, but she cautioned that not enough is yet known about the details.

Her biggest concern is that creating an academy modeled after the military service academies would conflate what NASA does—the peaceful, civil exploration of space—with military activities undertaken by the US Space Force.

“NASA’s charter and legal foundation calls for a civilian agency separate from the military,” Garver said. “Structuring a feeder college along the lines of a military academy strikes me as ill-conceived.”

Garver served under President Obama at NASA about a decade ago. Since then, she has been involved in the creation of several fellowship programs to funnel more women and minorities into aerospace engineering. She said NASA has not historically had difficulty attracting young talent into the space program, even if there is not as much upside in pay as there can be in the private sector. Traditionally, NASA has had close ties to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Purdue University, and other institutions that have long fed talent into the space agency.

Trump did not seek to dispel concerns along these lines during his remarks.

“So you think of West Point, and you think of Annapolis, and you think of the Air Force Academy, and you think of the Coast Guard Academy,” Trump said after announcing the Space Academy. “They’re all great, but we’re going to have now the Space Force.”

stories.title: Fed has 'work to do' if price rises don't ease for Americans, Warsh says
stories.summary: Kevin Warsh remarks suggest interest rates could be increased if policymakers think inflation is running too high.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 28 August 2026

The head of the US central bank has said policymakers will "have work to do" if they were not confident cost-of-living pressures were easing for Americans.

Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said while inflation readings looked better than expected over the summer, they did not show that the current picture had "meaningfully improved".

The new Fed boss stressed that his remarks should not be treated as a guide for future interest rate decisions, but the comments are a signal rates could be raised if policymakers believe inflation is too high.

Latest figures show prices rose 3.4% in the year to July, above the Fed's 2% target. Another inflation measure closely watched by the Fed is running at 3.7%.

Warsh made the comments in his first speech at the annual Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in Wyoming, which sees central bankers, government officials and academics from around the world gather to talk about interest rates, inflation and other economic issues.

Warsh said given prices were rising by more than 2% on an annual basis, "the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices".

"Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do."

The central bank boss has remained tight-lipped about the potential path of interest rates, but investors will have watched his speech closely for any signs of the Fed's approach under his leadership.

The central bank's next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September.

The reactions to any decision made by US President Donald Trump will be closely watched, with the mid-term elections looming and voters concerned about affordability.

Trump, who appointed Warsh in May, repeatedly criticised and pushed his predecessor Jerome Powell to cut interest rates. The president has previously said rate hikes "just keeps the country down".

Warsh issued a plea in his speech to not label his remark as "forward guidance" and said he believed the practice of sending signals to the markets on future interest rate decisions, adopted in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, had "overstayed its welcome".

"Oversharing policy deliberations and overcommitting to future decisions can lead markets, businesses, and households astray," he said, adding it also inhibited the Fed the "freedom to make the right calls when it's time to decide".

Interest rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row amid concerns over inflation due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.

Following Warsh's remarks, the rates market showed growing expectations of an interest rate rise in September, according to CME data.

Analysts at Capital Economics said Warsh's speech delivered a "far clearer - and hawkish - message" and that it left "the door open to a hike" earlier than previously expected.

"Hikes are not guaranteed, but Warsh is now at least suggesting he is on board with them if economic growth remains strong and monthly core PCE [Personal Consumption Expenditures] price growth remains a bit too firm," they said.

Why the US economy is ringing alarm bells Published 21 August

'No magic wand' to tackle high prices, Fed boss says as US interest rates held Published 29 July

Higher oil prices has also fuelled bond market investors, who have demanded higher returns, leading to higher borrowing costs for the US government and other major corporations.

Such borrowing costs impact the cost of borrowing for mortgages, car loans and credit cards.

The spike in interest payments has driven US national debt past the $40tn (£29.5tn). The figure has doubled in a decade under both the Trump and Joe Biden administrations.

The figure is rising by about $90,000 (£66,500) every second, or $7.8bn a day, according to the Congress Joint Economic Committee.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the government would buy back more debt in a bid to lower borrowing costs, but the market's reaction to the announcement proved short lived.

Interest rate hikes are a tool used by central banks aiming to slow the pace prices are rising in the shops. By pushing up the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, central bankers hope consumers will spend less and the rate of price increases will slow.

Higher interest rates, however, can lead to better returns for savers.
